## **1.0 Introduction**

Natural Resource Solutions Inc. (NRSI) was retained by International Power Canada, Inc. to conduct post-construction monitoring at the operational Harrow Wind Farm near the Town of Harrow, ON.  This wind energy production facility is made up of four 9.9MW (6 turbine) facilities.  The four facilities combine to represent 24 operational turbines with a total operational capacity of 39.6MW.  The project area and turbine locations can be seen in Figure 1.

The monitoring program undertaken at the Harrow Wind Farm was established through extensive discussions with Environment Canada (EC) and Aylmer District Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR), facilitated by Natural Resources Canada (NRCan).  These discussions resulted in an accepted _Harrow Wind Farm: Post-construction Follow-up Plan_ dated February 2010.  This final follow-up plan prepared by NRSI, and circulated to all agencies, can be seen in Appendix I.

Post-construction monitoring at the Harrow Wind Farm included fall bird behavioural surveys (focused on raptor migration), bird and bat mortality monitoring, and searcher efficiency and scavenger removal trials.  These surveys were conducted to assess the potential impacts of this wind energy production facility on local wildlife populations. Results of this full year of post-construction monitoring have been compared to the detailed pre-construction data collected by NRSI and Mr. Dave Martin, which were both summarized in the _Harrow Wind Farm: Environmental Screening Report_ (Helimax 2008).

The purpose of this report is to provide the detailed methodology and results from a full year of post-construction monitoring conducted at the Harrow Wind Farm.  This report summarizes the findings of avian studies and mortality monitoring, to assess the potential impacts of this facility, and provide recommendations for future monitoring.

For the purposes of this report, NRSI will frequently use the terms „mortality‟ and „carcass‟.  The term „mortality‟ will refer to dead birds and bats that were found in the vicinity of turbines at the Harrow Wind Farm.  The term „carcass‟ will refer to dead birds and bats that have been placed beneath wind turbines by NRSI staff for the purposes of searcher efficiency or scavenger removal trials.

## **2.0 Bird Behaviour Survey Methodology**

Given the potential usage of migrating raptors within the Harrow Wind Farm project area, Environment Canada has recommended, through comments provided on the Environmental Screening Report (ESR), that fall bird behaviour studies be conducted at the Harrow Wind Farm.  These surveys have been focused on the potential raptor activity near, and through, the project area, but document all bird observations during the monitoring period described below.  The purpose of these post-construction bird behaviour surveys was to assess any potential displacement or disturbance effects to avian species when compared with baseline information collected by Dave Martin during pre-construction avian studies.

## 2.1 Monitoring Period

Raptor migration activity peaks during the fall months, typically between the periods of mid-August and mid-October, depending on the species.  Based on this information and the monitoring period chosen for pre-construction avian studies, NRSI biologists conducted avian surveys during the period of mid-August to late October.  These surveys occurred on 11 dates on an approximate weekly basis from August 18 to October 27, 2010.  A summary of the monitoring dates, including pertinent weather conditions, has been provided in Table 1 below.

## 2.2 Monitoring Effort

During each of the 11 visits to assess bird behaviour at the Harrow Wind Farm, NRSI biologists conducted 30 minute surveys at 6 migration monitoring stations.  These 30 minute surveys were conducted between 1000-1600hrs, following the same preconstruction methodology used by Dave Martin.  This time period corresponds to the late morning and early afternoon periods when raptor migration activity for most species is expected to peak.

## 2.3 Survey Locations

The 6 migration monitoring stations surveyed on each visit corresponded to the same survey locations used by Dave Martin during pre-construction bird surveys, and represent a variety of habitats, geographical locations, and proximities to operational turbines.  All station locations, seen on Figure 2, were conducted at roadside locations throughout the overall project area.

Station BMM-001 is located southeast of the project area in Colchester, on the lakeshore at the marina.  BMM-002 is located on Erie Blue Beach Line, between County Road 50 and the lakeshore.  BMM-003 is also located south of the project location, on Wright Road just north of County Road 50.  Station BMM-004 is located on the east edge of the project area, on Dunn Road, just east of turbines T28 and T29.  BMM-005 is located within the centre of the wind project, on Fox Road just east of turbine T30.  BMM-006 is located west of the project area, at the intersection of County Road 41 and County Road 20.

## 2.4 Data Collection

During all avian behavioural surveys, NRSI biologists documented all bird activity that was observed.  For each bird (or flock) observation, all appropriate information, including species, number of individuals, flight direction, distance from turbine blades, etc. was recorded.  The data sheet used to collect this information has been included in Appendix II of this report.  Although all bird information was collected, there was a strong focus on raptor observations, which is reflected in the bird behaviour results (Section 4.0) of this report.

## **3.0 Mortality Monitoring Methodology**

## 3.1 Mortality Monitoring

## 3.1.1 Sample Locations

Although the Harrow Wind Farm is considered a medium sized facility (11-40 turbines), which would typically require a subset of turbines to be searched, comments received from Environment Canada requested all 24 turbines be searched during the monitoring period of August through October.  Comments received from the MNR indicated their comfort with a subset of 12 turbines being searched during the period of interest for bat activity (July through September).  As a result, NRSI biologists conducted mortality monitoring at a subset of 12 turbines during the month of July before increasing monitoring effort to search all 24 turbines during the months of August, September, and October.  Turbine sampling frequency has been outlined on Figure 3, which indicates the 12 turbines that were searched during the month of July 2010.  On isolated instances, biologists were not able to search particular turbines due to maintenance activities, inclement weather, or other safety concerns.

## 3.1.2 Monitoring Period and Search Frequency

The monitoring period for work at the Harrow Wind Farm was designed through the use of available guidance documents (EC 2007, OMNR 2007) and direct comments received from EC and MNR through Natural Resources Canada.  Based on a review of available materials and agency comments, two mortality monitoring periods were surveyed by NRSI biologists.

The period of summer swarming and fall migration for bats typically extends from midJuly through early September.  As a result, mortality monitoring surveys were conducted during the three month period of July through September that is expected to overlap with peak periods of bat activity in this area of the province.

Fall bird migration activity, with focus on raptor species, typically peaks during the months of August through mid-October.  As a result, NRSI biologists conducted mortality monitoring during the three month period of August through October.

In accordance with provincial and federal agency comments and recommendations, NRSI implemented a twice weekly search frequency during the entire monitoring period of July through October.  Although distinct time periods were chosen for specific activity periods, all bird and bat mortalities encountered during the full July through October monitoring period were documented and collected.

## 3.1.3 Sample Area

NRSI biologists conducted mortality searches within a 50m radius of the each turbine base.  Any mortality that was incidentally observed beyond the search radius was still documented, photographed, and collected appropriately.  Regardless of groundcover, agricultural crops, or other factors, biologists searched as much of the 50m radius as seemed reasonable during each survey.  Habitat mapping of the groundcover was completed in July, August, and October using the visibility classes recommended by the Ministry of Natural Resources.  Unsearchable areas, if any, were documented as such in habitat mapping (see Appendix VII).  To mark visibility class boundaries, NRSI biologists measured the distance of several points along the boundaries to the turbine base and mapped accordingly.  To calculate the percent area searched (Ps), the percent of the unsearchable area was calculated from the mapping using a grid overlay.

Mortality searches were conducted using linear transects, spaced approximately 5m apart.  In order to maintain consistent search efforts between searches, mortality searches were limited to approximately 20 minutes at each turbine.

## 3.1.4 Data Collection

During each visit to conduct mortality searches, all appropriate information was documented, including weather conditions, date, time, observer, and approximate operational speed of the turbine being searched (if applicable).  All data sheets used during the post-construction monitoring program can be seen in Appendix II.

In addition to general information collected on each visit, a variety of specific information was recorded upon encountering any mortality.  This detailed information, as shown on the data sheet provided in Appendix II, included species, sex and age of the individual (if identifiable), any apparent injuries, direction and distance from turbine base, substrate type and visibility class, and unique mortality identification number for future reference.

Specific UTM coordinates and photographs were also taken for each specimen to allow for further analysis.

## 3.2 Scavenger Removal Trials

As outlined in the work program prepared by NRSI, scavenger removal trials were conducted approximately once per month at the Harrow Wind Farm, occurring a total of 4 times.  During each of the scavenger removal trials, occurring in each of July through October, approximately 20 carcasses were placed throughout the Harrow Wind Farm, with 2 carcasses placed at each of 10 randomly selected turbines.  This sample size was chosen for this facility to limit the potential for attracting scavengers to turbine locations since all sites were being searched for mortalities.  Species, UTM coordinates, direction and distance from turbine base, and substrate were all noted during the placement of each specimen.

Carcasses included both bird and bat specimens, varying in actual ratios depending on availability of specimens, but generally in a ratio of 3 birds: 1 bat.  Bird carcasses included species native to this region of the province and ranged in size, including golden-crowned kinglet ( _Regulus satrapa_ ), magnolia warbler ( _Dendroica magnolia_ ), blue jay ( _Cyanocitta cristata_ ), and American woodcock ( _Scolopax minor_ ).  Based on comments received from the MNR, bat carcasses only included the three migratory species known to occur within Ontario, hoary bat ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ), silver-haired bat ( _Lasionycteris noctivagans_ ), and red bat ( _Lasiurus borealis_ ).  This selection of migratory bat species is an attempt to limit the spread of white-nosed syndrome in resident bat populations, wherever possible.

During each scavenger removal trial, the bird and bat carcasses were left for at least 7 days and were checked on each mortality survey at that turbine to address any scavenging or signs of scavenger presence.

## 3.3 Searcher Efficiency Trials

In conjunction with mortality searches, NRSI conducted numerous searcher efficiency trials on staff that were routinely conducting mortality searches at the Harrow Wind Farm.  Similar to scavenger removal trials, searcher efficiency trials were conducted approximately once per month to account for seasonal changes in groundcover.

Searcher efficiency trials were conducted on each searcher that assisted with mortality searches during the given monitoring period, and were conducted on a total of 6 dates during the entire monitoring period.  For each trial, searchers were tested without their knowledge, through the placement of approximately 20 test carcasses.  Carcasses were placed randomly within the project area at some or all of the turbines to be searched, and placed throughout the 50m search radius in all habitat types and visibility classes. Each test carcass was discreetly marked, and each found specimen was later compared to the total number of carcasses placed within the project area.

Searcher efficiency carcasses included a combination of birds, bats, and artificial bats (made from black hockey tape).  Fake bats were used in moderation at the Harrow Wind Farm based on preliminary indication from other studies that bats made from electrical tape or hockey tape provide an object similar to that of a bat mortality.  Bird carcasses used ranged in size and consisted of bird species native to this portion of the province, and only migratory bat specimens were used.  The exact ratio of carcasses used generally included 10 birds (ranging in size), 5 migratory bat carcasses, and 5 artificial bats, but depended on overall carcass availability.

## 3.4 Estimated Mortality

In addition to total bird and bat mortalities directly observed by NRSI biologists, an estimated mortality will be calculated on a per turbine and per MW basis using the following equation recommended by agency staff:

Corrected Mortality Estimates (C) = c / (Se x Sc x Ps)

C: the corrected number of bird or bat fatalities

C: the number of carcasses found

Se: the proportion of carcasses expected to be found by searchers (searcher efficiency)

Sc: the proportion of carcasses not removed by scavengers over the search period

Ps: the percent of the area searched.

The above formula has been used to address estimated mortality rates during specific time periods, locations, habitat types, or visibility classes, providing all variables used are specific to the desired criteria.  This can allow for estimated mortality rates for specific time periods (e.g. the month of August), at turbines in proximity to specific

habitat types, at specific turbine locations, etc, and will be extremely beneficial in identifying potential spatial and temporal risks to bird and bat populations.  Should apparent differences between searcher efficiency or scavenger results be observed between habitat types, visibility classes, geographic locations, or other variable factors, the above formula will be used separately for each appropriate set of conditions or variables.

Searcher efficiency and scavenger removal results will be incorporated into the above equation by using the equations detailed in Sections 5.0 and 6.0, respectively.  In addition to searcher efficiency and scavenger removal rates, NRSI biologists have also incorporated percent area searched (Ps in the equation above).  This variable represents the percentage of the 50m radius search area that was regularly searched for mortalities.  In most instances, the entire search area was examined for mortalities, however in certain locations habitat features, such as dense shrub thickets or watercourses, could not be searched and have been accounted for through this percent area searched variable.

## **4.0 Bird Behaviour Survey Results**

A total of 8,313 birds, representing 60 different species, were documented during fall avian surveys near the Harrow Wind Farm.  The most abundant bird species observed during these surveys was European starling ( _Sturnus vulgaris_ ).  The majority of these were observed in flocks at stations BMM-005 and BMM-006.  Results of the fall avian surveys have been discussed in more detail below.

## 4.1 Species Composition

During fall avian monitoring, NRSI biologists documented a total of 60 bird species near the Harrow Wind Farm.  The most abundant bird observations were European starlings, representing a total of 3,207 individuals, more than one-third of the total observations. These birds were primarily observed at the inland stations further from the Town of Harrow, BMM-005 and BMM-006, at distances of up to 600m from the observer.  Other species that were frequently documented during the fall monitoring period included common grackle ( _Quiscalus quiscula_ ), turkey vulture ( _Cathartes aura_ ), and ring-billed gull ( _Larus delawarensis_ ).  All species observed during 2010 avian monitoring at the Harrow Wind Farm have been incorporated into a detailed bird species list seen in Appendix III.

Landbirds were the most abundant bird group observed, accounting for 82% of all observations.  This is primarily a result of a number of large flocks (>100 individuals) of European starlings and common grackles, as well as many smaller flocks (10-50 individuals) of American goldfinches ( _Carduelis tristis_ ).  Waterbirds were the second most abundant bird group observed during fall 2010 avian surveys, which primarily consisted of ring-billed gulls and herring gulls ( _Larus argentatus_ ), accounting for a combined 8.8% of all observations.  Raptors accounted for 8.0% of all bird observations, largely consisting of turkey vultures.  Shorebirds and waterfowl each accounted for less than 1% of total observations.

Eight different species of raptors were observed within the Harrow Wind Farm during fall migration surveys.  In order of abundance, these included turkey vulture, sharp-shinned hawk ( _Accipiter striatus_ ), red-tailed hawk ( _Buteo jamaicensis_ ), northern harrier ( _Circus cyaneus_ ), American kestrel ( _Falco sparverius_ ), Cooper‟s hawk ( _Accipiter cooperii_ ),

osprey ( _Pandion haliaetus_ ), and bald eagle ( _Haliaeetus leucocephalus_ ).  An additional 22 individuals could not be identified to species due to height and distance from the observer, including one kettle of 21 unidentified _Buteo_ sp.  Turkey vultures and sharpshinned hawks were also the two most abundant species of raptor observed in preconstruction surveys (Martin 2007).

## 4.2 Station Distribution

When data was analyzed at each station separately, the majority of bird observations occurred at stations BMM-005 and BMM-006, in the center and northwest corner of the project area, where 66% of the total bird observations occurred during fall behaviour surveys.  These observations consisted primarily of large flocks of European starlings, common grackles, red-winged blackbirds ( _Agelaius phoeniceus_ ), brown-headed cowbirds ( _Molothrus ater_ ), gull species, and turkey vultures.

Observations of many gulls and small flocks of American goldfinches occurred at the monitoring stations situated closer to the shoreline (BMM-001, BMM-002, and BMM003).  Twenty-eight percent of the total observations occurred at these three stations combined.

## 4.3 Activity Patterns

When conducting avian surveys within the Harrow Wind Farm, biologists noted how close birds were flying to operational turbines, in order to assess any potential risk to bird populations.  Although most birds regularly maintained distances of more than 100m from turbine bases, some often flew as close as 15m to a turbine base.  A total of 7 birds, consisting of separate observations of individual birds, flew within 40m of the turbine base.  Included in these observations were 3 individual raptors (northern harrier, turkey vulture, and red-tailed hawk) which flew immediately below operational turbines. Raptors were also often observed flying at blade sweep height in the area.

In addition, nearly half (47.9%) of all raptors were observed flying directly west (270o) through the project area.  The majority of these observations were of turkey vultures, including one kettle of greater than 250 individuals observed on October 14[th] .  This is consistent with observations made by Dave Martin, who indicated that large raptors in this area tend to migrate in a path that travels parallel to the project area, heading in a

westerly direction to pass north of the Big Creek Marsh Life Science ANSI (Helimax Energy 2008).

The trend noticed by Dave Martin in which almost all of the small hawks observed ( _Accipiter_ species and American kestrels) are flying along the shoreline south of the study area was also observed by NRSI biologists in 2010 (Helimax Energy 2008). Eighty-seven percent of the small hawks were observed at stations BMM-001, BMM002, and BMM-003, and none of these observations were individuals located north of the turbines.  The majority of these observations were individuals or small groups flying northwest or southwest.

During fall 2010 raptor monitoring, no birds were observed changing flight or behaviour patterns around operational turbines, and no direct impacts (i.e. mortality) to birds were observed during these specific bird behaviour monitoring surveys.

## 4.4 Avian Monitoring Summary

Results of the 2010 avian monitoring studies at the Harrow Wind Farm indicate that concentrations of several hundred, or more, raptors are occasionally present, and individuals and small groups of raptors are regularly seen throughout the project area during the fall migration period.  Individual raptors were observed in very close proximity to turbines, even directly below the blades of operational turbines.  Landbirds were also seen in close proximity to turbine towers.  Large raptors appear to migrate westward across the centre and northern portions of the project area, and small raptors appear to travel closer to the lakeshore, south of the Harrow Wind Farm turbines.  Both of these migration patterns were observed during pre-construction monitoring surveys.  No changes in flight or behaviour were observed around operational turbines.

## **5.0 Scavenger Removal Trials**

Scavenger removal rates within the Harrow Wind Farm were found to be extremely variable, with months ranging from 95% of carcasses still remaining on the following mortality search to low as 60% of carcasses remaining on the following mortality search in September.  September scavenger removal trials were inadvertently conducted slightly differently than the other months (Table 2).  Carcasses during this trial were all placed on the same day (Day 0), instead of being placed on regular search days.  As a result, when each of the turbines was re-checked on the subsequent mortality search day, half of the turbines were checked on Day 2 and the other half on Day 3.  Scavenger trials during each of the other months involved carcasses being placed on regular search days, so even though half of the turbines are searched on the following day, this still amounts to the same search day, as seen in Table 2.  Details on the tester, date placed, species, distance and direction from turbine, dates checked, UTM, and whether the carcass was scavenged can be found in Appendix IX.

To address the scavenger removal rates for each of the specific monitoring periods, NRSI has used the general equation provided by the MNR and EC on other similar projects.  The equation is seen below:

SC: proportion of carcasses not removed by scavengers nvisit0: total number of carcasses placed nvisit1 – nvisit3: numbers of carcasses remaining on visits 1 through 3

## July 2010

Using the scavenger removal results, seen in Table 2, and the equation provided by agency staff, the July 2010 scavenger removal rate has been determined as follows:

SCJuly = (nvisit1 + nvisit2) / (nvisit0 + nvisit1)

= (13 + 8) / (20 + 13) = 21 / 33 = **0.64**

Based on the results of scavenger removal trials, approximately 64% of carcasses remained after the average search frequency of approximately 3 days during the month of July.

## August 2010

Using the scavenger removal results, seen in Table 2, and the equation provided by agency staff, the August 2010 scavenger removal rate has been determined as follows:

SCAugust = (nvisit1 + nvisit2 + nvisit3) / (nvisit0 + nvisit1 + nvisit2)

= (19 + 11 + 5) / (20 + 19 + 11) = 35 / 50 = **0.70**

Based on the results of scavenger removal trials, approximately 70% of carcasses

remained after the average search frequency of approximately 3 days during the month of August.

## September 2010

Using the scavenger removal results, seen in Table 2, and using an expansion of the recommended equation provided by agency staff, the September 2010 scavenger removal rate has been determined as follows:

SCSeptember = (nvisit1 + nvisit2) / (nvisit0 + nvisit1) = (12 + 9) / (20 + 12) = 21 / 32 = **0.66**

Based on the results of scavenger removal trials, approximately 66% of carcasses remained after the average search frequency of approximately 3 days during the month of September.

## October 2010

Using the scavenger removal results, seen in Table 2, and the equation provided by agency staff, the October 2010 scavenger removal rate has been determined as follows:

SCOctober = (nvisit1 + nvisit2) / (nvisit0 + nvisit1)

= (22 + 22) / (24 + 22) = 44 / 46

= **0.96**

Based on the results of scavenger removal trials, approximately 96% of carcasses remained after 3 days during the month of October.  Because the scavenger removal formula assumes a linear rate of carcass removal, NRSI does not expect a large difference in values between a study of short duration and one of longer duration. However, on recommendation by the Ministry of Natural Resources, the scavenger removal rate for September has been used for October as well.  It is therefore assumed that approximately 66% of carcasses remained after the average search frequency of approximately 3 days during the month of October.

Using the information calculated above, NRSI has determined that the appropriate scavenger removal rates, using recommended equations, and has provided these values in Table 3 below.

## **6.0 Searcher Efficiency Trials**

Searcher efficiency rates within the Harrow Wind Farm were relatively consistent throughout the monitoring period, ranging from 45% in September when soybean crops were tallest, to 85% in October after crops had been harvested and visibility was good. Although generally consistent, the searcher efficiency rates recorded during the summer 2010 monitoring period were relatively low, largely due to areas of tall soybean crops and wheat fields with dense red clover encountered within some of the project area. Results of these seasonal searcher efficiency trials are summarized in Table 4.  Details on the searcher and tester, species, distance and direction from turbine, habitat, substrate, visibility class, UTM, and whether the carcass was found or scavenged can be found in Appendix VIII.

## **7.0 Avian Mortality Results**

## 7.1 Avian Mortalities

During the mortality monitoring period at the Harrow Wind Farm, NRSI biologists found a total of 20 bird mortalities in the vicinity of operational turbines.  All but one of these observations was identified to the species level.  The bird mortality not identified to the species level was a result of scavenging activity that had removed most of the carcass prior to biologists being able to document it.  The 19 bird mortalities identified to the species level represented a total of 10 different species.  The most commonly found species were purple martin ( _Progne subis_ ) and horned lark ( _Eremophila alpestris_ ), with a total of 5 and 4 mortalities documented, respectively.  The other avian mortalities included no more than 2 of each of American robin ( _Turdus migratorius_ ), barn swallow ( _Hirundo rustica_ ), brown-headed cowbird, golden-crowned kinglet, mourning dove ( _Zenaida macroura_ ), ovenbird ( _Seiurus aurocapillus_ ), red-eyed vireo ( _Vireo olivaceus_ ), and tree swallow ( _Tachycineta bicolor_ ).  No raptor, waterfowl, waterbird, or shorebird mortalities were observed at the Harrow Wind Farm during the 2010 monitoring period.

Avian mortalities were observed at 14 of the 24 turbines, with no single turbine accounting for more than 3 individual mortalities.  Turbine T02 had the highest observed bird mortality with a total of 3 documented mortalities, of three different species.  Four other turbines, T04, T13, T24, and T36, each had 2 mortalities.  The same bird species was not found twice at any of the turbines throughout the monitoring period.  Individual turbine maps and specific mortality locations (UTM coordinates) are appended to this report (Appendix IV).

Temporal distribution of avian mortalities was generally consistent throughout the monitoring period with 4, 5, 5, and 6 mortalities documented in each of the monitoring months from July to October, respectively.  Observed mortalities were generally reflective of specific bird activity periods.  All 4 horned lark mortalities were observed between September 14 and October 21, 2010 when this species returns to wintering grounds in southern Ontario.  Expected resident bird species, including American robin, mourning dove, and barn swallow, were found throughout the monitoring period.  All 5 purple martin mortalities were found between July 6 and August 6, 2010, which is

expected to correspond to migration for this species, as peak migration for purple martins in the United States is known to occur in late July, August, and September (Brown 1997).

Details regarding each avian mortality, including date, time, location, and species are summarized in Appendix V.

## 7.2 Corrected (Estimated) Avian Mortality

Based on the field observations at the Harrow Wind Farm, NRSI biologists have compiled the searcher efficiency trials, scavenger removal trials, and direct mortality observations into an equation that will be used to estimate the total avian mortality at the Harrow Wind Farm.  The equation, based on recommendations received from EC and MNR is found below:

## **C = c / (SE*SC*PS)**

C: Corrected (Estimated) Mortality Rate c: actual observed mortalities SE: overall searcher efficiency SC: proportion of remaining carcasses PS: proportion of the total area searched

## **8.0 Bat Mortality Results**

## 8.1 Bat Mortalities

During post-construction mortality monitoring at the Harrow Wind Farm, NRSI biologists collected a total of 167 bat mortalities throughout the monitoring period, consisting of both resident and migratory bat species.  A detailed examination of bat mortalities at the Harrow Wind Farm has been included in the following sections.  Detailed information pertaining to each bat mortality observed during the 2010 post-construction monitoring at the Harrow Wind Farm can be seen in Appendix VI.

## 8.1.1 Species Composition

Bat mortalities observed by NRSI biologists represented a total of 5 different species, including little brown bat ( _Myotis lucifugus_ ), big brown bat ( _Eptesicus fuscus_ ), and all three migratory species, hoary bat, eastern red bat, and silver-haired bat.  Migratory species were more frequently encountered during mortality surveys, accounting for a combined 88.6% of all bat mortalities at the Harrow Wind Farm.  The eastern red bat and hoary bat were the most abundant bat mortality documented, representing 45.5% and 38.9% of all bat mortalities, respectively.  The two resident bat species observed during mortality surveys, big brown bat and little brown bat, each accounted for a considerably smaller proportion of total bat mortalities, representing 7.8% and 3.0%, respectively.  One bat mortality could not be identified to the species level due to advanced decomposition.  Observed species composition of bat fatalities can be seen in Figure 4 below.

**Figure 4.  Species Composition of 2010 Bat Mortalities at the Harrow Wind Farm**

## 8.1.2 Mortalities by Date

Bat mortalities were observed throughout the monitoring period, but were most abundant during the month of August 2010.  During this month, bat mortalities were considerably higher for three of the bat species, big brown bat, eastern red bat, and hoary bat.  More than two thirds of the total mortalities for each of these species were observed during the month of August.  The remaining two species, little brown bat and silver-haired bat, were noted in small enough numbers that no distinct temporal pattern was observed.  The daily mortality patterns of all bat species can be seen in Figure 5.

Mortalities of resident bat species were relatively few in number at the Harrow Wind Farm, and occurred throughout the monitoring period without any high mortality nights associated with either the little brown bat or big brown bat.

**Figure 5.  Seasonal Bat Mortalities at the Harrow Wind Farm**

Patterns of migratory bat mortalities appear to be generally consistent with the expected migratory time periods for Ontario‟s migratory species.  Hoary bats are thought to be a relatively early migrant within Ontario, which is consistent with the observation of 34 (52%) of all hoary bat mortalities observed between the period of August 3[rd] -20[th] , 2010. Similarly, the eastern red bat, a slightly later migrant, was observed in higher numbers from August 12[th] -27[th] , 2010.  During this time period 44 (51%) of the total eastern red bat mortalities were observed.  Although few silver-haired bat mortalities were observed they were found from August 20[th] to October 15[th] , 2010, suggesting a somewhat later migration through southwestern Ontario than other species.  The temporal pattern of migratory bat mortalities is shown in Figure 6.

**Figure 6.  Seasonal Migratory Bat Mortality at the Harrow Wind Farm**

## 8.1.3 Spatial Distribution

Bat mortality across the Harrow Wind Farm varied considerably between turbines, from a single bat mortality, observed at turbines T20 and T30, to 20 bat mortalities observed at turbine T14.  NRSI biologists have reviewed several aspects of the landscape, including pre-construction ELC mapping, provincial basemapping of natural features, proximity to shoreline, and general geographic position of turbines with higher mortality.

NRSI has noted that the group of 12 turbines that make up the large turbine cluster in the southwest of the project area have been observed to have the highest mortality rates.  The remaining turbines, although still responsible for a small number of bat mortalities, had consistently lower impacts than those in the southwest of the project area.  Six of the seven turbines with more than 10 mortalities each are located in the southwest group of 12 turbines.  These 6 turbines are located at the northwest (T1, T2, and T7) and southeast (T6, T14, and T12) ends of the subset of 12 turbines.  In addition,

the 7[th] turbine with more than 10 mortalities, T10, is located at the eastern end of northern group of 6 turbines.  The higher number of mortalities observed at these turbines may be a result of higher searcher efficiency due to the less vegetated ground cover.  However, this was not the case in all instances.  Regardless of ground cover, searcher efficiency and scavenger removal trials were conducted to account for any potential variation, and are integrated into the final corrected estimate.  Aside from this general geographic correlation, there is no direct indication that natural features, such as woodlots or watercourses, have had an influence on the number of bat mortalities observed within the project area.

The number of bat mortalities observed at each turbine, divided by species, can be seen in Figure 7 below.

**Figure 7.  Turbine Distribution of 2010 Bat Mortalities at the Harrow Wind Farm**

The highest observed impact on migratory bats was seen at turbine T14, where a total of 18 migratory bat mortalities were observed.  Turbines T01 and T07 each also accounted

for more than 10 migratory bat mortalities during the 2010 monitoring period.  Patterns of resident bat mortality are difficult to detect due to the relatively small number of resident bats affected.  However, a slightly elevated number of big brown bats (n=4) was observed at turbine T10.

Bat mortalities were observed at all distances from the turbine base, from <1m to beyond the 50m search radius.  Based on the observed results of this study, it is clear that most of the bat mortalities observed by NRSI were found within 50m search radius, and more than 90% of all observations were observed within 40m of the turbine base. ## **9.0 Summary and Conclusions**

## 9.1 Raptor Surveys

During 2010 avian studies conducted at the Harrow Wind Farm, NRSI biologists documented a total of 8,313 birds, representing a total of 60 different species.  The most abundant birds observed during this monitoring period were European starlings, representing greater than one-third of all of the individuals observed.  Landbirds were the most abundant bird group observed, accounting for 82% of all observations.  When data was analyzed at each station separately, the majority of bird observations occurred at stations BMM-005 and BMM-006, in the center and northwest corner of the project area, where 66% of the total bird observations occurred during fall behaviour surveys. These observations consisted primarily of large flocks of European starlings, common grackles, red-winged blackbirds, brown-headed cowbirds, gulls, and turkey vultures.

The target species of these surveys, raptors, were observed occasionally in high concentrations, and individuals and small groups were regularly seen throughout the project area during the fall migration period.  Individual raptors were observed in very close proximity to turbines, even directly below the blades of operational turbines.  Large raptors appear to migrate westward across the centre and northern portions of the project area, and small raptors appear to travel closer to the lakeshore, south of the Harrow Wind Farm turbines.  Both of these migration patterns were observed during preconstruction monitoring surveys conducted by Dave Martin (Helimax Energy 2008).  No changes in flight or behaviour were observed around operational turbines.

## 9.2 Avian Mortality

A total of 20 avian mortalities were documented within the Harrow Wind Farm during the 2010 monitoring period.  Based on the total observed avian mortalities, searcher efficiency rates, scavenger removal rates, and equations recommended by applicable agencies, a total corrected (estimated) avian mortality rate of 2.73 birds/turbine/year (1.66 birds/MW/year) has been determined for the Harrow Wind Farm.  Based on the observed avian mortalities, the potential impact of this facility will be largely focused on resident species and common migratory songbirds.  No mortalities of any provincially or

federally significant species, raptors, waterfowl, or shorebirds were observed during the first full year of mortality monitoring in 2010.

Results from a two-year study at the Erie Shores Wind Farm, near Port Burwell, ON, has resulted in an estimated avian mortality rate of between 0.41-2.6 native birds/turbine/year (James 2008).  Another Ontario study, conducted at the Melancthon I Wind Plant, indicated an estimated avian mortality rate of 1.4 birds/turbine/season (Stantec Consulting Ltd. 2008).  The Ripley Wind Power Project estimated an avian mortality rate of 3.12 birds/turbine/year (Jacques Whitford Stantec Ltd. 2009), and the Wolfe Island EcoPower Centre estimated an avian mortality rate of 6.99

birds/turbine/year (Stantec Consulting Ltd. 2010).  Based on these studies at similar facilities in Ontario, the results at the Harrow Wind Farm suggest avian mortality rates that are consistent with, or lower than, other estimated avian mortality rates within Ontario.  Similarly, a study of mortality monitoring at a variety of wind energy facilities in North America has suggested a range of avian mortality rates between 0.63-7.7 birds/turbine/year or 0.95-11.67 birds/MW/year (Arnett et. al. 2007).  The results of the Harrow Wind Farm (2.56 birds/turbine/year or 1.55 birds/MW/year) are within the lower portion of this North American range of avian mortalities.

The results of 2010 mortality monitoring indicate a low level of concern regarding direct impacts (mortality) to avian populations at the Harrow Wind Farm.

## 9.3 Bat Mortality

A total of 167 bat mortalities were documented during the 2010 mortality monitoring period at the Harrow Wind Farm.  Based on the total observed bat mortalities, searcher efficiency rates, scavenger removal rates, and equations recommended by applicable agencies, a total corrected (estimated) bat mortality rate of 18.36 bats/turbine/year (11.13 bats/MW/year) has been determined for the Harrow Wind Farm.

Migratory bats were the most impacted species, with mortalities of eastern red bat representing 45.5% of the total observed bat mortalities, followed by the hoary bat at 38.9%.  Mortalities of silver-haired bats, little brown bats, and big brown bats were also observed within the project area in variable numbers.  Big brown bats were the resident species most impacted by the operational turbines (8% of total observed mortalities).

Similar facilities in Ontario, including the Erie Shores Wind Farm and Melancthon I Wind Plant have shown lower estimated bat mortality rates.  Results from a two-year study at the Erie Shores Wind Farm resulted in an estimated mortality rate of 1.05-5.8 bats/turbine/year (James 2008).  Results from the Melancthon I Wind Plant also indicate lower estimated bat mortality rates of approximately 4.2 bats/turbine/season (Stantec Consulting Ltd. 2008).  The Ripley Wind Power Project reported a higher estimated mortality rate of 12.99 bats/turbine/year (Jacques Whitford Stantec Ltd. 2009), and the Wolfe Island EcoPower Centre reported an estimated mortality rate of 14.77 bats/turbine/year (Stantec Consulting Ltd 2010).  A summary of available literature, prepared by the OMNR (2006) identifies a range of bat mortalities at North American facilities from approximately 0.07 bats/turbine/year to over 47.5 bats/turbine/year.  Other literature review studies suggest similar ranges of 0.5-69.6 bats/turbine/year or 0.7-53.3 bats/MW/year (Arnett et. al. 2007).  Results documented during the 2010 postconstruction monitoring at the Harrow Wind Farm indicate that the impacts of this facility occur within the mid-range of estimated North American mortality rates.

Species composition at the Wolfe Island EcoPower Centre indicated that the migratory species hoary bat and red bat were the most often encountered during mortality surveys, respectively (Stantec Consulting Ltd. 2010).  These species composition results are similar to those observed at the Harrow Wind Farm, where red bats and hoary bats were also the two most abundant species observed.  Hoary bats were also the most abundant species of bat mortality observed at the Ripley Wind Power Project, although the second highest species encountered was the resident little brown bat (Jacques Whitford Stantec Ltd. 2009).  Many wind energy facilities across North America have documented higher mortality rates of migratory species (Arnett et. al. 2007), similar to the results at the Harrow Wind Farm.

Although 2010 mortality monitoring at the Harrow Wind Farm has resulted in a bat mortality rate within the mid-range of estimated North American mortality rates, the bat mortality rate at the Harrow Wind Farm is above the threshold of 10 bats/turbine/year or 4.5 bats/MW established by the MNR in 2010 for “potential negative environmental effects” (OMNR 2010).

## **2.0 Purpose**

The purpose of post-construction monitoring at the Harrow Wind Farm is to verify the accuracy of the environmental assessment of the project, with special focus on bird and bat activity and to determine the effectiveness of any mitigation measures that are implemented to mitigate adverse environmental effects of this project.

The _Canadian Environmental Assessment Act_ (CEA Act) also requires that the results of follow-up programs may be used for implementing adaptive management measures or for improving the quality of future EAs. It will then be possible to identify the impact of this wind energy facility on the avian and bat populations that utilize the Harrow area.

The plan will ensure that any unanticipated potentially significant adverse environmental effects are detected and addressed so that they do not become significant. The adaptive management strategy contained in Section 8.2 of this Plan provides further details on how this is accomplished.

## **3.0 Bird Behaviour Surveys**

Given the potential usage of migrating raptors within the Harrow study area, Environment Canada has recommended, through comments provided on the ESR, that bird behaviour studies be conducted at the Harrow Wind Farm following the same protocol undertaken in pre-construction surveys. Pre-construction raptor surveys were conducted to establish raptor use and general flight heights in the study area. The purpose of the post-construction raptor use surveys is to assess potential displacement or disturbance effects (i.e., distribution and abundance) to these species compared to pre-construction conditions.

## 3.1 Monitoring Period and Effort

Raptor migration activity peaks in the fall months, typically between the periods of midAugust and mid-October depending on the species.  NRSI will conduct eleven surveys occurring between late August and the end of October while the wind farm is operational (2010).  These surveys will be conducted once per week during the late August to late October time period for the total of eleven visits. The protocol to be followed is outlined below:

During each of the proposed visits to assess migratory raptor behaviour around operational turbines, 30 minutes will be spent at each of the six migration monitoring stations within the Harrow Wind Farm study area.  Surveys will occur between 10001600hrs when raptor activity is expected to peak.  The order that stations are monitored on each visit will be rotated so each station is monitored during different periods during the day to assess spatial and temporal variations in raptor activity.  For each bird observation, all appropriate information, including species, number of individuals, flight direction, distance from turbine blades, etc. will be recorded.  Although surveys will focus on raptor activity, all bird observations will be documented during each surveys.  This methodology is consistent with pre-construction avian monitoring conducted for this project, and will allow for detailed comparisons between the pre-construction and postconstruction results.

## 3.2 Survey Locations

In order to make accurate comparisons between pre-construction monitoring and postconstruction monitoring results, the same six survey stations that were used in the preconstruction monitoring effort will be used. These are anticipated to provide adequate coverage of the study area, and will provide sightlines to all twenty-four turbines within the Harrow Wind Farm area.  The proximity of some of these monitoring locations to the shoreline of Lake Erie will also allow for observations of the activity of migratory raptors along the shoreline immediately south of the study area.
